content: Folic acid is an FDA-approved nutritional agent used for the treatment of megaloblastic anemia caused by folic acid deficiency. It is also effective in anemias of nutritional origin, as well as those associated with pregnancy, infancy, or childhood. Oral administration is preferred, as most patients with malabsorption can absorb folic acid when given orally, even if they cannot absorb food folates. However, doses exceeding 1 mg daily should not be used unless vitamin B12 deficiency has been ruled out or is being adequately treated with cobalamin. Higher doses do not enhance hematologic effects and are mostly excreted unchanged in the urine. The usual therapeutic dosage for adults and children is up to 1 mg daily, although resistant cases may require larger doses. Patients should be closely monitored, and maintenance levels adjusted if relapse appears imminent. In conditions such as alcoholism, hemolytic anemia, anticonvulsant therapy, or chronic infection, maintenance levels may need to be increased. Folic acid is contraindicated in patients with a known intolerance to the drug. It is not appropriate as sole therapy for pernicious anemia or other megaloblastic anemias caused by vitamin B12 deficiency, as it may obscure the diagnosis by improving hematologic symptoms while allowing neurological complications to progress. This can result in severe nervous system damage before the correct diagnosis is made. Adequate vitamin B12 supplementation can prevent, halt, or improve these neurological changes. Adverse reactions to folic acid are rare but may include allergic sensitization, such as erythema, skin rash, itching, general malaise, and respiratory difficulty due to bronchospasm. Gastrointestinal side effects, including anorexia, nausea, abdominal distension, flatulence, and a bitter or bad taste, have been reported in patients receiving high doses (e.g., 15 mg daily for one month). Other side effects include altered sleep patterns, difficulty concentrating, irritability, overactivity, excitement, mental depression, confusion, and impaired judgment. Prolonged folic acid therapy may decrease serum vitamin B12 levels. In some epileptic patients, folic acid has been reported to increase seizure incidence when taken with anticonvulsants like phenobarbital, primidone, or diphenylhydantoin. Folic acid is rapidly absorbed from the small intestine, primarily in the proximal portion. It appears in the plasma within 15 to 30 minutes after oral administration, with peak levels generally reached within one hour. It is metabolized in the liver to tetrahydrofolic acid derivatives, which are distributed to all body tissues but stored primarily in the liver. Normal serum folate levels range from 5 to 15 ng/mL, and levels below 5 ng/mL indicate deficiency. Levels below 2 ng/mL are typically associated with megaloblastic anemia. During pregnancy, folic acid requirements are significantly increased, and deficiency can result in fetal damage. Folic acid is excreted in the milk of lactating mothers, and supplementation may be necessary for low-birth-weight infants, breastfed infants of mothers with folic acid deficiency, or those with infections or prolonged diarrhea. Folic acid tablets are supplied as 1 mg doses and contain inactive ingredients such as lactose monohydrate, microcrystalline cellulose, sodium starch glycolate, and stearic acid. They should be stored at 20° to 25°C (68° to 77°F) in well-closed containers protected from light.
